The first topic is artificial intelligence, or AI.
AI is the big umbrella.

So deep learning is a special type of machine learning.

objects in the pictures.

=== Building Generative AI Chatbots ===


--- Transformer - architecture ---

Welcome back.
In the last lesson, we explored large language models, what they are and how they work at a high level.
Now in this lesson, we are going to dive into the concept of transformer architecture.
The actual design that powers almost all modern llms like GPT, Gemini, and Llama.
Every advanced large language model you have heard of is built using transformers.
So before transformer architecture came into picture and before all these large language models, right,
the natural language processes and tasks such as it can be a translation of text or some text generation.
Everything is done by a type of neural network called a recurrent neural network or RNN.
So when the LLM came into picture this is completely revolutionized.
So let's understand how LLM kind of does this.
So processes entire sentences at once not word by word.
So earlier model specifically RNNs.
Right.
So they read text one word at a time.
And that was slow and not very good at capturing the entire context.
Transformers changed this by looking at the entire sentence all at once and not word by word.
It is like instead of reading a book through a small keyhole, word by word, you suddenly open the
whole door and you see the full page.
So that's the idea of Transformers, and they are powered by self-attention that captures the word importance
and context.
So self-attention is the secret sauce in the transformer models.
It helps the model figure out which words are more important.
For example, this is like a famous, uh, statement or the text that we have in this process of transformer
architecture.
You will see this example a lot.
The cat sat on the mat.
This is the sentence.
I'll repeat this again.
The cat sat on the mat.
The model knows cat relates more closely to SAT than to the words like the or on or something like that.
So cat is more related to sat, which is which are kind of the important words.
Right.
So all these important words are identified by using this concept called as self-attention.
And then we have this origin.
We had a paper called attention is all you need.
So this is the origin of this transformer architecture.
And this paper was kind of proposed in 2017 by Google.
So this descent came from a famous research paper.
As I said, this is the title which is Attention is all You Need.
And then again, this paper introduced the transformer and it completely changed the field of AI.
And it was initially proposed for machine translation or translation text from one language to other.
So that's the first use case it was proposed on.
And later it was adapted to text generation from some user queries.
And then we have, uh, this transformer architecture excels at translation text generation and more.
Because of this design, transformer are excellent at tasks like these things translation or summarizing
a large text, generating new text, and even writing code.
So these are some of the applications that transformer kind of add.
And that's what we are using in current world, like the main applications of large language models.
So now let's talk about two, you know, core components of a transformer model, which are encoders
and decoders.
So the encoder converts input text into rich contextual embeddings through multiple stacked layers.
Each layer combines self-attention and feed forward networks, enabling bidirectional processing for
complete contextual understanding.
So this is the definition.
Maybe you can note it out.
And I've just like broken down this definition in smaller points.
But now I'll explain this in simple terms.
So uh, the encoder is the part of this transformer that reads and understands the input text.
It turns word in words into rich numerical representation called embeddings, basically converting text
into numbers and what we call as embeddings.
Because as we know that the models and the machines understand numbers and not text, right.
So it also uses a multi layers of self-attention.
Basically it is a neural network.
So it uses multi layers of self-attention to capture deeper meaning and it's bidirectional.
So when it when we say bidirectional bidirectional, it just means that it looks at the whole sentence
from both directions, left to right and right to left to understand the context in the full view.
So that's about encoder.
So I'll just repeat this core stuff again.
So your encoder just like takes this input text and it understands this input text converts this into
numerical representation called as embeddings.
And the multi-layer self-attention is used in order to understand the importance and the meaning of
this words.
And it is bidirectional so that it understands like words like from both the way so that it can understand
the context better.
And then we have decoder.
So the decoder generates output sequence step by step using masked self-attention to preserve casualty
and cross-attention uh, and integrate encoder information, ensuring coherent and contextually accurate
outputs.
So let's understand this.
So the decoder is the part that generates the output.
Think about encoder as the part that understands the input and decoder is the part that generates the
output.
So the decoder predicts one word at a time or one token at a time.
And then we have this concept called as mask attention.
So it uses mask attention so that the model doesn't cheat by looking at words ahead in the sentence.
So it shouldn't do that.
Rather it should predict the words one by one.
So that's why the masked self-attention concept is used and it uses cross-attention.
So cross-attention is basically to connect with encoders understanding of the input text so that it
can give you a better output.
In simple words, I'll just like give you a statement that you can remember.
Think of it like this.
The encoder is the reader that carefully studying the input, whereas the decoder is the writer creating
the answer one word at a time, but based on what the reader understood.
So that's all about it.
So encoder is a reader, decoder is a writer, but the writer also takes into account of what the encoder
understand from the text.
So that's how you can remember this.
So now let's discuss about the self-attention mechanism which is a core concept of this transformer
model.
So the purpose of this self-attention mechanism, it allows the model to weigh the importance of each
word in a sequence relative to all others, enabling rich context understanding.
So basically this just means that each word looks at every other word and decides which words matter
most for the context.
So it's like if you give it a sentence with several words, the self-attention mechanism should identify
the important words and the meaningful words and the relationship between that.
And then we have this query key value.
So we have self-attention uses query key and value vectors from input embeddings via linear projections
to model the relationship between tokens.
So what this means is the model uses these three things query, key, and value for each word.
These are just ways to compare words with each other and calculate how strongly they are related.
So all these I think this is simplified, right?
Just think about think about this as like how we calculate how the words are related to one another.
So for this these factors, such as query, key and value for each words are kind of used.
And then we have this attention computation.
So the model then produces the score that tell it how much attention to give to each word.
So more attention is let's say, given to uh, the important words that are like contextually important
in that sentence.
Maybe let's consider an example.
Let's say there is a sentence called as she poured water into the cup because it was empty.
In this case, the word it should pay more attention to cup than to water.
That's what attention scores figure out.
Like which words should be, you know, should give the attention to which word.
So that is like the key factor here.
So this is about the concept of self-attention mechanism.
And basically like what it does.
And then we have another important concept called as positional encodings.
Transformers.
Look at all words at once.
So they need a way to know the other the order of words in a sentence.
Since as we have discussed earlier, right?
Transformers process every words in parallel.
They don't naturally know because of this, right?
They don't naturally know if a word comes first, second, or last.
But word order is critical in order to understand the input text.
Let's say we have a statement called as man bites dog.
This is very different from a statement like dog bites man as the transformer is transformer model is
understanding or reading this entire words together.
It doesn't know which comes first.
So that's why the positional encoding is important.
To solve this we add positional encodings.
It's like a signal that marks each word with its position.
So that way the model understands both the meaning of the words and their order.
Okay, so self-attention is all about just finding the important factors or the important words in a

Positional encoding gives you that positional awareness of in which order the words are present in a
sentence.
Okay, so that's that's about it.
So that's what I've given in this sentence as well.
And then we have the training process.
Transformers are first trained on huge amounts of text pre-training and then adjusted for specific tasks
called as fine tuning.
They learn in a self-supervised way, using methods like filling in missing words, masked language
modeling, or predicting the next sentence.
By seeing billions of words, they pick up grammar, meaning, and patterns in language, which makes
them useful for many applications.
So basically, transformers are first trained on billions of words to learn language in general.
So it kind of gets this generic understanding of that language.
And this is what we call as pre-training.
So it is trained with like volumes of data like a huge volume of data.
And after that we have a process called as fine tuning like specific smaller data set.
So the task can be a chat application.
So it then fine tuned on chat based data set.
Or it can be like understanding the code.

=== Capstone Projects – Build and Deploy Real-World AI Solutions ===


--- Accessing LLMs via LangChain ---

In this lesson, we will explore how to access different llms like OpenAI's GPT Llms, Google's Gemini,
grok, open Source, Llms, and Llms using a single framework called Long Chain.
So what is long Chain?
Long chain is an open source Python framework designed to make it easier to build applications with
Llms.
It provides a unified interface to connect with different models, but it also goes beyond just LLM
API calls.
It includes tools for prompt chaining, conversation memory, connecting llms with external data, building
pipelines, and so on.
Now, why is this better than just calling APIs directly through an OpenAI library or a Google AI library,
and so on?
Because with long chain, you don't have to juggle four different SDKs.
You get one consistent way to talk to multiple models, and at the same time, you get access to advanced
features that save a lot of development time.
Think of Long Chain as a universal adapter and toolkit for working with Llms and building large language
model applications.
By the end of this video, you will see how long chain not only simplifies working with Llms, but also
sets the foundation for building real world AI applications much faster.
So let's get started.
So I'm going to run the Python code on JupyterLab.

--- Using Prompt Template ---

Welcome to section four.
Prompt engineering.
So far we have looked at the foundation of generative AI, how models like Transformers work, and then
how to actually access different llms in Python using APIs and frameworks like Lang chain and Lambda
index.
But the real magic happens in how we talk to these models.
This is where prompt engineering comes in.
Prompt engineering is the art and science of crafting the right instructions to guide an LLM towards
accurate, useful and structured outputs.
In this section, we will explore the different ways to design prompts like how to use prompt templates
to make your prompts reusable and consistent, how to get results with zero shot prompts where the model
answers without examples, and how to improve responses with few prompts by showing the model.
Some demonstrations and examples.
Let's start with prompt templates, the building blocks of structured prompting.
So a prompt template is basically like a blueprint for your prompts.
Instead of writing the full instruction manually every time.
For your LM call, you create a template with placeholders or in other words, variables that can be
dynamically filled in with context and user input or some information.
So you don't have to write this entire prompt again and again.
Rather, we can have these placeholders getting filled in.

--- Zero-shot Prompting ---

Prompting is when we give the LM a clear instruction and let it generate the response directly.
We don't provide any examples or demonstration.
The LM works only with the prompt itself.
It's the simplest form of prompting and very useful when you need quick, direct answers.

--- Understanding RAG ---

Welcome to section six retrieval augmented generation, also called Rag.
In the last section we have seen how to build chatbots using Lang chain and Lama index powered by large
language models.
But there is still one major challenge with Llms.
They don't always know everything and sometimes they even make things up.
Rag is the technique that solves this problem.
Let's understand it step by step in this section.
First, let's understand the idea behind rag before we start building with it.
Large language models face key limitations when relying only on pre-trained data without external knowledge
access during inference.
So what this basically says is large language models or llms are trained on a huge amount of data,
but once training is complete, their knowledge becomes frozen.
This leads to three main problems that I have listed here.
They may give incorrect or made up answers when they do not know something.
So basically the response will be incorrect or fabricated.
They may also provide outdated information because the training data might be months or even years old,
and they can't always point to a trusted source for the answers that they are generating.
So the answer is kind of unverified.
Now RAC comes in as a solution.
So instead of just relying on the model's memory and, you know, the training data it was trained on.
Rag allows the model to look things up in real time.
So retrieval augmented generation overcomes these challenges by connecting llms to trusted external
sources in real time.
Okay, so this is what Rag basically means.
So when you are using Rag, these limitations are kind of solved by these three key factors.
So you get the most accurate and correct information that you pass as in the form of like documents,
text and so on.
And you also attach answers to trusted sources.
So there is always source attribution.
And it also avoids retaining the whole model every time new data comes in, right?
So you don't have to retrain the model again and again as like the data is getting changed because now
you are giving the context to the model in the form of these documents.
Okay.
So this is how Rag solves this problem that we have discussed over here.
So Rag basically gives LLM a knowledge upgrade from external knowledge sources or documents.
So now let's understand like about how this rag works and like what exactly it is.
Okay.
So the idea is simple.
Before the model answers your question, it retrieves relevant information from a knowledge base and
then uses that to generate a response.
Okay.
So that's what I have given here.
Rag enhances large language model outputs by retrieving and grounding them in authoritative external
knowledge sources, improving accuracy, reliability, and factual consistency.
Think about giving a documentation and asking it to answer it from there instead of, you know, answering
it from the data it was trained on because it was trained on the data that is present in the internet
and some information on the internet can be wrong, right?
So instead of that, we are giving it trustable source documents and we are asking it to answer it from
there.
So that's the core concept of RAC.
And these are the key benefits of this.
So the answer will always be more reliable and factual.
The answer will also be up to date as we can provide it like latest documents and like documentations.
And the model can also provide domain specific knowledge like, you know, uh, legal, medical or company
data, which might not be present in the internet when it was trained on.

--- Building a RAG system in Python with Llamaindex ---

In the last lesson, we built a rack system using long chain where we ingested PDF documents, stored
them in chroma DB, and then retrieved relevant chunks to generate accurate answers.
Now we are going to do the same process with llama.
Llama index is another popular framework for retrieval augmented generation, but its focus is slightly
different compared to long chain.
While long chain is great for building flexible pipelines and chaining multiple components, Llama index
is designed specifically around data ingestion, indexing, and querying.
That means when it comes to Rag, it often feels more streamlined and beginner friendly.
And when you are working on projects in organization, you will see that people would generally prefer
llama index over long chain when it comes to Rag applications.
So in this lesson, we will again break it down into two steps document ingestion and retrieval generation
process.
In document ingestion, we will load and split the PDF documents, then create an index out of it,
and in the next step of retrieval and generation, using that index that we have created, we will fetch
the relevant chunks and generate context aware answers using Llms.
By the end, you will see how Lama index can make Rag workflows simpler and easier to manage compared
to, you know, long chain, especially if your main goal is connecting Llms with external documents.
So let's get started.
I have my Jupyter Lab ready over here, and I have added this Rag architecture diagram that we have
seen.
So we have that entire process that we have discussed in the previous lessons.
So we have a knowledge base that would be chunked into smaller pieces.
And this data chunks or text chunks is converted into vector embeddings using a embedding model.
And this embedding.
Let's say let's call this as document embeddings are basically vector representation of the text in
simple words numerical representation of the text data.
So these document embeddings are saved in a vector db.
And in the next flow when the user asks a question.
This question is also converted into a vector embedding using the embedding model.
Let's call this as query embedding.
And then we run a similarity search on this vector db where we retrieve the relevant text for this,
uh user query.
And we get that retrieved documents.
Now this relevant uh content for this user query, as well as the content, is kind of sent to the LLM
in the form of a prompt.
And the LLM would kind of finally answer the question.
And the main point to note here is we are not sending that vector representations to the LLM.
Rather, we are actually sending the text once we retrieve the relevant chunks.
Once we run the similarity search algorithm on the vectors, we actually retrieve the text format of
data, and we only send like the user query and the retrieved chunks in text format to LLM.

--- Understanding AI Agents ---

Welcome to section seven AI agents.
Over the last few years, large language models have become very powerful, but they are still limited
in a way.
They mostly generate responses when you ask them something.
Now the focus is shifting towards AI agents, which are emerging as one of the most exciting areas in
generative AI today.
Instead of just responding, agents can think, plan and take action.
They can use tools, access knowledge, work with APIs, and even collaborate with other agents to achieve
complex goals.
That's why companies and researchers are calling this the next big step in AI.
If Llms were like the brain agents are like the brain, plus the ants capable of actually doing the
work.
So in this lesson we will understand what agents are.
Explore their core components.
Look at real world applications of AI agents, and then dive into different frameworks like pedantic
AI, Microsoft, Autogen, Landgraf and crew.
AI and we will also understand how to build AI agents using these frameworks.
So this will be the agenda for this seventh section.
So what are AI agents?
AI agents are autonomous software systems that perceive their environment, make decisions, plan and
take actions to achieve specified user defined goals.
So you have a user defined goal and the agent thinks, makes decision and take action to perform or
achieve that specific goal.
And they are an autonomous software system.
This definition is like pretty self explanatory.
Maybe you can just like take a note of this.
And unlike chatbots, right.
Which just respond agents can actually execute tasks.
For example, if you ask a chatbot book me a ticket, it might might just tell you how to book a ticket.
But an agent can go ahead, open the booking system and actually do it for you.
In short, agents don't just answer, they do the actual work.
So before we go further, let's clarify a small but important point.
The difference between AI agents and agent AI.
So AI agents are the individual systems that perceive reason and act.
Think of them as autonomous digital workers.
And then we have agentic AI.
Agentic AI is kind of the broader trend or approach in generative AI, where we design systems to be
more proactive, interactive and action driven rather than being passive.
So this will be achieved by coordinating multiple AI agents to achieve complex goals.
In simple terms, right Agentic AI is the movement and AI agents are the building blocks for that movement.
So that's like the clear difference between them.

First is autonomous.
Autonomous thing is like their key characteristic.

goal oriented.
They plan and complete multi-step tasks to achieve that goal.
They are adaptive, they learn from feedback and adjust their actions according to the feedback that
they get.
And then collaborative.
They can work with humans, or even they can collaborate with multiple agents to form a multi-agent
system.
That's what makes them much more powerful than traditional AI systems.
So now let's understand about the core components of an AI agent.
So first is perception gathering information.
So perception is how the agent understand its environment.
It gathers information from different sources like user input documents APIs or data streams.
For example, when you ask an AI assistant for today's weather, it's perception is taking in your request
and also pulling in external weather data.
And without this perception, the agent wouldn't know what's happening around it.
So that's like a very core component and idea behind the AI agents.
And then we have reasoning and planning.
This is where the LLM part comes in.
Once the agent has information it needs to decide what to do next.
This is where reasoning and planning comes in.
And the agent uses the large language model, or LLM, to break down the problem into smaller steps
and plan an approach.
For instance, if you ask an agent to organise a meeting, it reasons first check your calendar, then
find available time slots, then send invites.
This ability to plan makes the agent proactive rather than being reactive.
And then we have are the tools part.
Tools extend the power of an agent and it is a very important factor of building an agent.
So tool to extend the power of an agent and agent on its own is limited.
But when it connects to external apps and services, it becomes far more capable.
Say, for example, a calculator tool for solving math problems.
A web browsing tool for fetching live information because Llms cannot access real time information,
right?
So a browsing web browsing tool can help that.
A company database tool for fetching internal data.
So this is why modern agents are often called tool using AI because tools give them superpowers.
And then we have memory.
Memory is what makes an agent smarter over time.
It can remember previous conversations, past actions, or long term goals.
For example, if you tell an AI assistant or let's say if you told an AI assistant your favorite restaurants
last week, memory helps it.
Recommend them again today, like without you repeating it.

Recommend it again today without you have to saying that this is my favorite restaurant that I want
to go.
And there are like two main key things here short term memory which keeps track of the current task.
And we also have a long term memory component that stores knowledge across multiple sessions and interactions.
So this makes the agent feel more personal and consistent instead of starting fresh every time.
And then finally we have action.
So reasoning alone is not enough.
Using these tools and everything is not enough.
The agent must be able to take an action.
Action means actually carrying out the steps, calling APIs, sending emails, updating a database,
or executing commands.
Think of it like the hands of the agent.
This is how it does the real work, not just talk about it.
So if perception is about understanding and reasoning is about planning, action is about getting things
done by using your tools and understanding the memory and everything.

So async just means Python can do more than one thing at a time.
It's like doing things in a parallel way, like without waiting.
For example, if it's waiting to download a file, let's say it can also answer another request instead
of just sitting idle till the file is downloaded.
To make this work, Python uses something called as an event loop, and you can think of this event
loop like a playground where tasks take turns quickly so it feels like they are all playing at once.
But here's the catch in Jupyter Notebook that playground is already running in the background.
If we try to start another one.
Python gets confused and throws an error.
That's why we use this nest async IO dot apply.
It's just a fix that tells Python don't build a second playground, just share the one that's already
running.
This way our async code and Jupiter.
Both of these can run together without problem.
So what it just tries to do is like some of the libraries, like just like this Pydantic and even Llama
Index sometimes want to run this in this event loop because of the async operations.
But in Jupiter notebook, as I said just now, there is an event loop that is already running here.
We are just saying that use the existing event loop.

--- Multi-Agent system with CrewAI ---

Welcome back.
So far we have seen how to build single AI agents using frameworks like pedantic AI and Microsoft Autogen.
Now it's time to step into something more advanced multi-agent systems.
In this lesson, we will be using AI, a framework designed to coordinate and manage multiple agents
working together.
AI is all about teamwork.
Instead of one agent trying to do everything, you can assign different roles to different agents and
let them collaborate to reach a goal.
To make this more concrete, we will be building a multi-agent trading system.
Here's the setup for this.
A stock research agent, which is responsible for analyzing market data for a given stock, and a trader
agent, which takes that research and decides whether to buy, sell, or hold a particular stock.
And we will also be building a custom tool that provides real time stock information to support their
decisions.
This example will show you how crew AI enables agent to communicate, share knowledge and combine their
strengths with other agents.
Something that's very difficult to achieve with just a single agent.
So by the end of this lesson, you will understand how multi-agent collaboration works in practice and
how crew AI makes it possible in a very easy way to implement this as well.
To design complex, role based AI systems that can tackle real world tasks.
Once you understand the basics, we will move on and try to build more advanced multi-agent systems
with crew AI.

--- Running LLMs Locally with Ollama & Docker ---

Welcome to section eight LM deployment.
So far we have been running large language models on our own machines.
But here's the thing many open source llms are too large to fit on a laptop, and even smaller ones
need to be deployed if we want to share them with others or use them in real applications.
In this section, we will start with Olama and Docker, which is not only useful for local testing,
but also extremely important in production setups.
Docker ensures everything runs the same way on any machine, your laptop, a server or the cloud.
Removing it works on my machine problem.
From there, we will move to the cloud with AWS, EC2 and we will also explore Run Pod, which gives
you access to cost effective GPUs and also look into VLM for faster serving of big large language models.
And finally, build a fast API layer to expose our Llms as Rest APIs.
By the end, you will know how to take open source models to a production ready environment that anyone
can access and any applications can access.
In this lesson, first lesson of this section eight, we will run open source LMS locally using Docker.
Now why Docker?
Sure, you could install Olama directly as we have seen earlier, right?
But in production setups that quickly becomes a headache.
Different machines, operating systems and dependencies can all break things.
Docker fixes this by packaging everything the model needs into a container that runs the same everywhere.
That means what we test locally is exactly what will run later on a cloud server.
It also makes scaling and managing large models much easier.
So let's start small running olama in Docker locally, and then we will be ready to move to bigger deployments

--- Deploying Ollama LLMs on EC2 with Docker ---

In the last lesson, we launched our very first AWS EC2 instance, a computer in the cloud.
But right now it's just an empty machine.
The next step is to actually run our LMS on it and connect it from our local machine.
To do that, we will set up inside Docker on our EC2 instance.
Remember why Docker is so powerful?
It gives us a consistent production ready environment.
So the same setup that worked on our laptop will work in the cloud too.
Once this is done, we will be able to pull and run open source LMS on EC2 models.
That might be too big for a personal computer, but run smoothly on cloud hardware.
This forms the foundation for the latest tips, where we will be adding a fast API layer, and the moment
we build a larger A applications in our capstone project section, we will understand how you can package
that entire application into multiple Docker containers and deploy it on EC2.
So this is going to form the basis for that.
So let's get started.
I am logged in into my AWS Management console.
So here I can find EC2 because I have already viewed it.

--- vLLM - High-Performance Serving on EC2 ---

So far, we have deployed Olama with Docker on our EC2 instance and successfully run open source Llms
in the cloud.
That's a big step forward.
But here's the catch as models get bigger, we also need them to run faster and more efficiently.
This is where VLM comes in.
VLM is a specialized serving engine that's designed to make open source Llms much more efficient.
It can handle large batches of requests, reduce memory usage, and significantly improve throughput
and latency compared to a basic setup.
In this lesson, we will set up VLM on our EC2 instance and see how it can serve open source Llms in
a way that's both scalable and production ready.
This will give us the performance we need when we are working with open source large language models.
So in this lesson, let's dive in and bring high performance serving to our EC2 instance.
So as we have discussed in the previous videos, I have created an EC2 instance and I'm connected to
that EC2 ubuntu instance from my local machine so we can go from there.

launch the EC2 instance from AWS, right?

It's pretty simple and it gives us like the base proper way of how to deploy VLM there.

--- Serve Local LLMs (Ollama) via FastAPI ---

In the previous lessons, we have been running our large language models locally inside an olima container.
That works fine if you are just typing commands directly into the terminal, or trying some basic questions
for the LLM to answer.
But in real world projects, models are almost never used this way.
Instead, they are served through an API layer which allows other applications to talk to them.
Here's why this is important.
Think about front end integration.
Suppose you are building a chat interface with Streamlit or let's say, a full fledged front end, uh,
tool like react.
The front end can't directly talk to the model.
It needs an API endpoint that accepts user input and returns model responses.
Fast API provides exactly that bridge.
And then we have scalability and extensibility.
Once the model is behind an API, you can add features like authentication, logging, or even chain
model with other services like databases, vector storage, etc. without touching the front end code.
And now, if you want to move this front end to a different tool, the back end is not affected so that
we have like a separate front end and a separate back end as well.
And then production ready.
This is how large systems are built in industry models wrapped with APIs, then consumed by apps, dashboards
or other backend services as well.
Later in the course, when we move on to the projects section, we will see how to take this a step
further by dockerizing both the model and the fast API, together with Docker Compose where you would
have like multiple Docker compose managed there.
But for now let's focus on the foundation for that.
Serving our local LMS via Fastapi and exposing endpoints that a frontend or any client can use.
So let's get started.
So the old model will be uh running here right.
So the LMS are still going to run on Olama, but we are not going to directly pass this to a front end
application.
Rather, we are going to see how we can wrap this up in a fast API server and just like, give them
the fast API endpoints that they can use.

--- Understanding MCP ---

Welcome to section nine, where we are going to talk about something that is generating a lot of hype
right now in the generative AI ecosystem, the Model Context Protocol, or MCP.
MCP is often described as the USB C of AI applications.
Think about what USB C did for technology.
Instead of carrying multiple chargers and connectors for every device, USB-C gave us one universal
connector that just works everywhere.
MCP brings that same simplicity to AI applications today.
When we build generative AI applications, we struggle because every model, every tool, and every
provider has their own way of working that makes integration slow, painful, and expensive.
MCP is a standard that solves this particular problem.
It creates a common language for AI models and tools to talk to each other, and in this section we
will first understand model context protocol, then see how to build an MCP server and finally use MCP
servers as tools, with agents built using pedantic AI and crew AI.
By the end of this section, we will clearly see why MCP is such a game changer for AI development.
So in this part, in this first part, let's really break down what MCP is, understand why it matters
and how it changes the way we build AI applications.
So before MCP was there like before it was launched.
Here are the key challenges every generative AI developer face.
First is the integration issue.
So we call this the m into n problem.
Imagine you have five tools and five different AI models.
To make them all work together.
You need 25 custom integration every time you add a new tool or a model.
The number of connections grows rapidly.
This is called the M problem and it slows down development massively.
And then we add no common standard.
Every provider, right.
Whether it's OpenAI or anthropic or uh, Gemini or an open source model as its own API style and data
format.
That means developers keeps writing custom glue code again and again, and then we add security gaps.
Sharing data safely across different tools is tricky, and without a standard protocol, each integration
has to reinvent how permissions, data access and security are handled.
Now let's look at what MCP brings to the table.
So MCP is an open source standard created by anthropic.
So I've mentioned it here.
They are also the one who created, uh Claude LM so yeah, they developed a model context protocol or
MCP.
And this is a open source standard.
And it gives us a unified plug and play way for large language models to use external tools, APIs and
data sources.
So now instead of rewriting integrations of different tools and agents and memory knowledge sources
and everything, you can connect everything once using similar MCP or the model context protocol.
And the benefits are huge.
You have a universal connector just like a USB-C.
It works everywhere and then easier scaling.
So no more M into n explosion of integration issues.
And then you have controlled data access.
So you decide exactly what tools and data the AI can use.
So this is why developers are calling MCP a breakthrough.
It makes AI development simpler, faster, and safer.
So, uh, now let's discuss about the core components of a model context protocol.
So MCP is built around these three core components.
One is your MCP host.
And then we have MCP client and then we have MCP server.
So first let's understand about this MCP os.
So I've given kind of a definition but I'll just explain this in words.
You can listen to this.
But later when you kind of want to revise this you can just like look at these slides that I would provide.
So first let's understand about this MCP host.
So this is the environment where the AI model or the LLM or even the application runs.
Say for example you have Cloud Desktop or you have an IDE like VS code or even a custom AI application,
or let's say we have, uh, GitHub Copilot.
So this is an AI, AI application or you have like Ides, like VS code, PyCharm and everything.
Right.
So this is an example of an MCP host where mainly your application resides or your LLM runs.
So the host is like the control center that connects the user to different tools and data sources via
MCP.
And then we have a MCP client.
MCP client is the bridge between the MCP host and the MCP servers.
So the job of the MCP client is to handle all communication, uh, turning requests and responses into
MCP standard format.
You can think of it like a translator that makes sure everyone speaks the same language.
And then we have MCP server, one of the most important component in this.

preserved there.

--- Project 3 - AstraRAG - Deploy locally with Docker ---

In the previous lesson, we have successfully created the back end and front end for our Agentic RAC
chatbot.
The next step is deployment.
The one way of deploying this is following what we have done for the last two projects, where we would
push this code to GitHub and pull this on an EC2 instance and just follow a bunch of process and deploy
it.
Right.
But there is a much more standard and followed practice which is using Docker.
So if you are new to Docker, just do a little bit research on why Docker deployment is better.
I'll just give you a quick idea.
But again, if you are new to this, just do some research.
Just try to understand like you know the advantages of this.
I'll just give you a overview.
So think about having this application right.
So we have this RAC chatbot.
So we use Python.
We use uh you know uh a library Lama index and so on.
In most cases what happens is if there is another person who is also want to try my code?
Okay, so I developed this on my Mac mini system.
So it's a mac OS.
If there is a person who is using the same code that is present in GitHub that I have pushed on a windows
machine, there is a chance that some libraries and some softwares may not work, or there can be some
dependencies they have to install separately in order to avoid that, in order to address those conflicts
and address this part where they don't have to install new softwares.
We deploy this application in a Docker container which basically packages the entire application.
Okay.
So just look at this definition here.
Docker deployment involves packaging and running applications within isolated environments called containers.
This process ensures consistency across different environments from development to production.
So that's the main idea.
So here I'm developing this in my local machine.
But when I'm deploying this on production there can be several issues that can go wrong.
A library can work in my Mac OS system or a windows server or a windows machine, but may not work in
an EC2 instance to avoid all these issues.
To have this consistency throughout development and production, we can containerize or package this
application in a Docker container.
Okay, so that's the main application of it.
And in order to build this there are like three key things.
One is a Docker file which is mainly like a recipe of how you would create a Docker image.
So in this Docker file you would say that I want this Python version, I want all these libraries,
this is the script that you need to run and so on.
So I would mention that uh, recipe of how to build the Docker image.
So Docker image is kind of like a template that has like all the data that the application needs.
And from this Docker image that you are building you can create any number of containers.
So these containers think about these as packaged individual applications that you have built.
So here we have built the agent chatbot right.
So we first design a Docker file and then we create a Docker image from it.
And from this Docker image you can create any instance of this uh chatbot that lives inside a Docker
container, and that is, like, isolated.
So that's the main idea of this.
So in this code that we have created, I'll show you how you can do that.
So first let's create a file I'll go to this new and create this Docker file.
So you can see it in PyCharm as well.
If you're not you can like install the extension, the plugin that's available.
Uh you will see this Docker file uh with this symbol over here.
So I'll add this.
And this is the name of the file without any extension d c k e r file docker file with d as uppercase
